Reading Fiction and Narrative: Plot
The sequence of events making up a story
Exposition
The opening that introduces setting, characters, and situation
Rising action
Events that build tension toward the climax
Climax
The turning point of highest tension in a story
Falling action
Events following the climax that lead toward resolution
Resolution
The ending where conflicts are settled
Protagonist
The central character whose goals drive the story
Antagonist
The force or character opposing the protagonist
Internal conflict
A struggle taking place inside a character's mind
External conflict
A struggle between a character and an outside force
Point of view
The perspective from which a story is told
First person
Narration using I, told by a character in the story
Third person omniscient
Narration knowing the thoughts of every character
Characterization
The methods an author uses to reveal a character
Reading Nonfiction and Informational Tex: Central idea
The main point a nonfiction text develops
Supporting detail
Evidence or explanation backing the central idea
Text structure
How information is organised, such as cause and effect or compare and contrast
Author's purpose
Whether a text aims to inform, persuade, or entertain
Objective writing
Writing based on facts rather than personal feeling
Subjective writing
Writing shaped by personal opinion or perspective
Bias
A slant favouring one side of an issue
Primary source
A firsthand record from the time being described
Secondary source
A later account analysing or interpreting events
Summarizing
Restating only the essential points in a much shorter form
Inference
A conclusion drawn from evidence rather than direct statement
Credibility
How trustworthy and reliable a source is
Introduction to Poetry: A grouped set of lines in a poem
The regular rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables
The pattern of end rhymes, labelled with letters
A comparison using like or as
A direct comparison stating one thing is another
Giving human qualities to something nonhuman
Language appealing to the five senses
An object standing for a larger idea
The voice delivering the poem, not necessarily the poet
Poetry without a fixed meter or rhyme scheme
A word imitating the sound it names
Drama and Shakespeare: A drama ending in downfall, usually of a noble protagonist
A drama with a light tone and a happy resolution
A protagonist whose flaw leads to their own ruin
The defect in character causing a hero's downfall
A speech delivered alone, revealing private thoughts
A remark to the audience unheard by other characters
A long speech delivered to other characters
The audience knowing something a character does not
A character whose contrast highlights another character's traits
Five unstressed-stressed pairs per line, Shakespeare's usual rhythm
The major and minor divisions structuring a play
Instructions in the script for movement, setting, or delivery
Grammar and Sentence Structure: A word group with a subject and verb that stands alone
A word group with a subject and verb that cannot stand alone
Two independent clauses joined by a conjunction or semicolon
An independent clause joined to a dependent clause
Two independent clauses joined without proper punctuation
Two independent clauses joined by only a comma
An incomplete sentence missing a subject, verb, or full thought
Matching a verb in number to its subject
A joining word such as and, but, or, so
A word such as because or although that starts a dependent clause
A noun phrase renaming the noun beside it
Using the same grammatical form for items in a series
Vocabulary and Word Study: A word part added to the front that changes meaning
A word part added to the end, often changing part of speech
The core carrying the base meaning of a word
Surrounding words that hint at an unfamiliar word's meaning
The literal dictionary definition of a word
The emotional association a word carries beyond its definition
A word with nearly the same meaning as another
A word with the opposite meaning
Words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning
The origin and history of a word
A phrase whose meaning is not literal, such as break the ice
The Writing Process: Planning and generating ideas before drafting
Rapidly listing ideas without judging them
A structured plan of a piece before writing it
Producing a first version, focused on getting ideas down
The final check for surface errors
Feedback from another reader before finalising
Adjusting writing to fit who will read it
The sentence stating the main idea of a paragraph
A word linking ideas, such as however or therefore
The closing that reinforces the main point without simply repeating
Narrative Writing: A piece of writing that tells a story
The time and place in which events happen
How quickly or slowly a story moves
Conveying meaning through detail and action rather than statement
Description drawing on sight, sound, smell, taste, or touch
A scene returning to an earlier moment in time
Early hints of events still to come
The emotional atmosphere created for the reader
The underlying message or insight a work conveys
A true story drawn from the writer's own life
The shape of a story from setup through climax to resolution
Expository Writing: One sentence stating the main claim of an essay
A paragraph developing one supporting point
Facts, examples, or quotations supporting a claim
Explaining how evidence supports the point being made
Examining similarities and differences between subjects
Explaining why something happened and what followed
Explaining how something works or is done, step by step
A neutral voice avoiding personal opinion
Ideas connecting logically so a reader can follow
Every sentence supporting a single main idea
Language appropriate for academic or professional writing
Research and Citation Basics: Research question
The specific question an investigation sets out to answer
Source evaluation
Judging whether a source is reliable, current, and relevant
Database
A searchable collection of vetted articles and references
Citation
A credit identifying where information came from
In-text citation
A brief source reference placed within the writing
Works Cited
The alphabetical list of sources at the end of a paper
Plagiarism
Using another's words or ideas without credit
Paraphrasing
Restating a source in your own words, still cited
Direct quotation
A source's exact words placed in quotation marks
Common knowledge
Widely known facts that do not require citation
MLA format
The citation style typically used in English classes
Note-taking
Recording key information and its source while researching
